1	**HARGROVE, STERN & WHITFIELD LLP** 1700 K Street NW, Suite 1200 Washington, DC 20006
2	
3	**MEMORANDUM**
4	
5	**TO:** Catherine \"Kate\" Ashford, Partner **FROM:** Benjamin Torres, Senior Associate **DATE:** April 11, 2025 **RE:** Protective Order Precedents from Recent FTC Merger Investigations --- Application to FTC File No. 241-0187 (Whitmore Logistics Holdings, Inc. / Cascade Regional Freight, Inc.)
6	
7	**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT** This memorandum is protected by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. It is prepared in anticipation of litigation and for the purpose of providing legal advice. Do not distribute outside the firm without prior authorization from the responsible partner.
8	
9	**[I. Introduction and Purpose]{.underline}**
10	
11	This memorandum summarizes protective order provisions negotiated beyond the FTC\'s standard form in three recent FTC merger investigations and identifies precedent-supported modifications to the proposed protective order circulated by FTC Staff Attorney Jonathan Heller on April 2, 2025, in connection with the Commission\'s investigation of the proposed acquisition of Cascade Regional Freight, Inc. by Whitmore Logistics Holdings, Inc. (FTC File No. 241-0187).
12	
13	The FTC\'s proposed order is eighteen pages in length, comprising twenty-two numbered paragraphs plus a definitions section and signature blocks. As currently drafted, the proposed order establishes only two tiers of confidentiality protection: \"Confidential Information\" and \"Highly Confidential Information --- Outside Counsel Only.\" The deadline for submission of a joint proposed protective order --- or, if the parties and Staff are unable to agree, competing proposals --- to the FTC is **April 25, 2025**.
14	
15	During the April 8, 2025 joint call with FTC Staff --- attended by our team, Pemberton & Locke LLP (Alan Hsiao and Sarah Leong, counsel for Cascade), and FTC Staff including Staff Attorney Jonathan Heller and Assistant Director Rebecca Muñoz --- Staff indicated a willingness to consider \"reasonable modifications\" to the standard form but expressed a strong institutional preference for the standard-form order. Staff specifically noted that any proposed modifications should be supported by precedent from recent FTC practice and should not impede the Bureau\'s ability to conduct its review.
16	
17	This memo focuses on **six specific areas** where the proposed order either departs from current market practice or fails to address significant risks presented by this investigation: (1) FRE 502(d) clawback protections, (2) challenge procedure deadlines, (3) treatment of confidential information in subsequent administrative or judicial proceedings, (4) expert and consultant conflicts screening, (5) three-tier confidentiality structures, and (6) derivative materials provisions.
18	
19	The context of this investigation warrants particular attention to protective order terms. Production volumes are substantial: the combined estimated production from both parties is approximately 1.88 million documents (approximately 12.6 million pages) from seventy-six custodians, including structured data such as pricing databases, route-level cost data, and financial models. Whitmore Logistics Holdings, Inc. (a 38-state freight and logistics operator, NYSE: WLHI) and Cascade Regional Freight, Inc. (an 11-state Western regional freight and last-mile delivery operator) have overlapping operations in the Portland-Vancouver, Seattle-Tacoma, Boise, and Sacramento metropolitan statistical areas, with combined market shares ranging from approximately 34% in Sacramento to approximately 52% in the Portland-Vancouver MSA. The degree of direct competitive overlap, the sensitivity of the information to be exchanged, and the substantial likelihood that this investigation could escalate to either an administrative proceeding or a federal court action under Section 13(b) all counsel in favor of robust protective order provisions negotiated at the outset.
20	
21	**[II. Summary of Precedent Matters]{.underline}**
22	
23	The analysis in this memorandum draws on the protective order provisions negotiated in three recent FTC Bureau of Competition merger investigations, each of which proceeded through the Second Request stage and involved modifications to the FTC\'s standard-form protective order. The three matters are summarized below for reference.
24	
25	**Matter A --- In re Thornfield Industries, Inc. / Beckett Supply Co.** (FTC Docket No. 9412, 2023). This investigation involved the proposed merger of two industrial distribution companies with overlapping regional operations. The parties were direct competitors in several geographic markets, and the investigation was handled by the FTC\'s Mergers II Division. Production volumes were approximately 1.5 million documents combined. The parties negotiated a modified protective order that included, among other things, a three-tier confidentiality structure, an extended challenge procedure deadline, and FRE 502(d) clawback language.
26	
27	**Matter B --- In re Galveston Health Partners, LLC / Meridian Ambulatory Group, Inc.** (FTC Docket No. 9428, 2024). This investigation involved a merger of two healthcare services providers. The investigation was particularly sensitive because it involved highly confidential patient-pricing data, payer-specific reimbursement rates, and econometric models prepared by the parties\' economic experts. The protective order included novel provisions for expert access, a derivative materials provision, and a bridge provision for subsequent proceedings.
28	
29	**Matter C --- In re Crestline Packaging Corp. / Durango Container Holdings, LP** (FTC Docket No. 9435, 2024). This investigation involved the acquisition of a PE-backed packaging and container manufacturing company. The matter was handled by the FTC\'s **Mergers IV Division** --- the same division handling the Whitmore/Cascade investigation. The protective order addressed third-party investor materials, post-investigation information handling, a three-tier confidentiality structure, and comprehensive FRE 502(d) clawback provisions. The involvement of Mergers IV makes this precedent particularly persuasive for our purposes.
30	
31	In each of the three matters, FTC Staff initially circulated the standard-form protective order, and in each instance, the parties successfully negotiated modifications beyond the standard terms. The precedents are discussed in detail in the sections that follow.
32	
33	**[III. FRE 502(d) Clawback Protections]{.underline}**
34	
35	Paragraph 16 of the FTC\'s proposed order includes a standard inadvertent production and clawback provision. Under the current language, a producing party that discovers it has inadvertently produced privileged or work-product-protected materials must promptly notify the receiving party, and the receiving party must return or sequester the materials and all copies within five business days. While this provision addresses the mechanics of clawback, it does not invoke or reference Federal Rule of Evidence 502(d), and this omission creates a significant gap in protection.
36	
37	FRE 502(d) provides that a federal court may order that the privilege or work-product protection is not waived by disclosure connected to the litigation pending before that court. Critically, a 502(d) order is binding on and enforceable against all persons and entities in all federal and state proceedings --- not merely the proceeding in which the order is entered. Without an operative 502(d) order, an inadvertent production of privileged materials during the FTC investigation could be seized upon by a third party in subsequent litigation --- whether a parallel private antitrust action, a state attorney general investigation, or even a Section 13(b) federal court proceeding initiated by the Commission --- as a basis for arguing that the privilege has been waived. A contractual clawback provision, standing alone, binds only the parties to the agreement and does not carry the force of a court order enforceable against non-parties.
38	
39	The risk in this matter is substantial. Given the massive production volume --- approximately 1.88 million documents comprising roughly 12.6 million pages from seventy-six custodians --- the probability of inadvertent production of privileged materials is high, notwithstanding rigorous privilege review protocols. Whitmore alone will be producing from forty-seven custodians (approximately 1.2 million documents, approximately 8.5 million pages), including documents from its 2022--2024 tuck-in acquisitions in the Pacific Northwest corridor that may contain third-party privileged communications inherited through those transactions and not yet fully catalogued. Cascade\'s twenty-nine custodians (approximately 680,000 documents, approximately 4.1 million pages) present similar privilege-review challenges, particularly with respect to communications with outside advisors in connection with the proposed transaction.
40	
41	**In Thornfield / Beckett (Matter A, Docket No. 9412),** the parties negotiated a provision expressly stating that the protective order was intended to constitute an order under FRE 502(d), and that the parties agreed to jointly move any court of competent jurisdiction for entry of a 502(d) order if the matter proceeded to federal court. FTC Staff in Mergers II initially resisted the language but ultimately accepted it on the understanding that the 502(d) provision would not alter Staff\'s substantive rights under the protective order or limit Staff\'s ability to challenge privilege designations through the order\'s existing challenge procedures.
42	
43	**In Crestline / Durango (Matter C, Docket No. 9435),** the protective order included a belt-and-suspenders approach: (a) express 502(d) language incorporated directly into the protective order itself, (b) a commitment by all parties to jointly seek a 502(d) order from the presiding Administrative Law Judge if an administrative complaint were filed under Part III of the Commission\'s Rules, and (c) a commitment to jointly seek a 502(d) order in any Section 13(b) federal court proceeding. FTC Staff in Mergers IV --- the same division handling our matter --- accepted this language without material objection.
44	
45	A practical complication warrants noting: FRE 502(d) by its terms requires a \"federal court\" order. An FTC administrative proceeding is not a federal court proceeding, and accordingly, a protective order entered solely by an Administrative Law Judge may not technically qualify as a 502(d) order under the Rule. The belt-and-suspenders approach used in Matter C addresses this limitation by preserving the parties\' right to seek a federal court order if the matter transitions to a judicial forum, while also ensuring that the protective order itself reflects the parties\' shared intent to prevent waiver by inadvertent production.
46	
47	**Recommendation:** We should propose adding language to Paragraph 16 expressly invoking FRE 502(d) and stating that the protective order is intended to constitute a 502(d) order, combined with a joint-motion commitment for any subsequent administrative or judicial proceeding. Matter C provides direct precedent from Mergers IV and should be cited in our markup.
48	
49	**[IV. Challenge Procedure Deadlines]{.underline}**
50	
51	Paragraph 18 of the proposed order establishes the procedure for challenging confidentiality designations. Under the current language, a party that believes a document has been over-designated must first engage in a meet-and-confer process with the designating party. If the dispute is not resolved within five business days of the initial written challenge, the challenging party must file a motion with the Commission within **ten business days** after the close of the meet-and-confer period. This deadline is unreasonably short given the scale and complexity of this investigation.
52	
53	The combined estimated production in this matter is approximately 1.88 million documents. Confidentiality designation disputes will inevitably arise in volume --- particularly given the extensive overlap between the parties\' operations and the breadth of competitively sensitive materials being produced. Preparing a meaningful motion to challenge designations requires marshaling specific evidence as to why particular documents or document categories do not warrant the level of protection assigned, drafting supporting declarations from individuals with knowledge of the documents\' contents and competitive significance, and addressing the applicable legal standards for each contested designation. Accomplishing this within ten business days is impractical, particularly when outside counsel are simultaneously managing Second Request compliance, witness preparation, and substantive advocacy on a parallel track. The ten-business-day deadline effectively discourages legitimate challenges and allows over-designation to go unchecked.
54	
55	**In Thornfield / Beckett (Matter A, Docket No. 9412),** the parties negotiated an extension of the challenge deadline from the standard ten business days to **twenty business days**. Staff in Mergers II initially resisted the modification but agreed after the parties demonstrated that the combined document volume in that matter (approximately 1.5 million documents) made the shorter deadline unworkable. The modified order in Matter A also included a provision --- absent from the FTC\'s proposed order here --- expressly stating that existing confidentiality designations remain in full force and effect during the pendency of any challenge motion, ensuring that the producing party\'s protections are not overridden before a decision is rendered.
56	
57	**In Galveston Health / Meridian (Matter B, Docket No. 9428),** the parties negotiated a **fifteen-business-day** deadline with an automatic ten-business-day extension available upon a showing of good cause. The modified order in Matter B also explicitly provided that the burden of proof rests on the designating party to justify its designation --- which is the standard approach in federal court protective orders but was not expressly stated in the FTC\'s proposed form in that investigation or in the proposed order here. Making the burden allocation explicit removes ambiguity and provides a clear framework for adjudication of designation disputes.
58	
59	Both Matter A and Matter B included explicit language providing that designations remain in full force during the pendency of any challenge. The FTC\'s proposed order in our matter is entirely silent on this point, creating a risk that a challenged designation could be treated as void or unenforceable pending resolution of the dispute. This gap exposes the producing party to the very harm the confidentiality designation was intended to prevent.
60	
61	**Recommendation:** We should propose extending the challenge deadline to twenty business days, adding a provision that all designations remain in full force and effect during the pendency of any challenge motion, and including an express allocation of the burden of proof to the designating party. During the April 8 joint call, FTC Staff signaled flexibility on the challenge procedure timeline, and this modification should be among the easier items to negotiate.
62	
63	**[V. Treatment of Confidential Information in Subsequent Administrative or Judicial Proceedings]{.underline}**
64	
65	The proposed order is entirely silent on the treatment of confidentiality protections if the FTC challenges the Whitmore/Cascade transaction by filing an administrative complaint under Part III of the Commission\'s Rules of Practice or by seeking a preliminary injunction in federal court under Section 13(b) of the FTC Act. This silence creates a critical gap. If the investigation escalates to an enforcement action, documents produced under the investigation-stage protective order could be placed on a public administrative record or filed in a public federal court docket without any confidential treatment, absent a separate protective order negotiated and entered in the subsequent proceeding. The transition from investigation to litigation creates a window of vulnerability during which the most competitively sensitive materials could be exposed.
66	
67	This gap is particularly consequential for the Whitmore/Cascade investigation. The FTC\'s preliminary concerns center on concentration in four overlap MSAs --- Portland-Vancouver, Seattle-Tacoma, Boise, and Sacramento --- with combined market shares as high as 52% in the Portland-Vancouver corridor. If the Commission elects to challenge the transaction, any resulting administrative proceeding or federal court action would be high-profile and would attract substantial attention from competitors, customers, and industry analysts. There is significant risk that competitively sensitive materials --- including Whitmore\'s \"Project Atlas: Western Expansion Strategy\" board presentation, which contains forward-looking pricing strategies, competitive assessments, and expansion plans for the overlap markets, and Cascade\'s customer-level profitability data, which reflects customer-specific margins, retention rates, and churn economics --- could become part of a public record, causing irreparable competitive harm regardless of the ultimate outcome of the enforcement action.
68	
69	**In Crestline / Durango (Matter C, Docket No. 9435),** the parties negotiated a **\"bridge provision\"** (Paragraph 21 of that order) specifically addressing this transition. The bridge provision stated that: (a) all confidentiality designations made under the investigation-stage protective order survive the issuance of any administrative complaint or the filing of any Section 13(b) action and remain in full force and effect; (b) the parties agree to negotiate in good faith a supplemental protective order for any such subsequent proceeding within fourteen calendar days of its initiation; and (c) pending entry of a supplemental protective order in the subsequent proceeding, the terms of the investigation-stage protective order continue to govern the treatment of all materials produced thereunder. FTC Staff in Mergers IV accepted this language, reportedly because it was seen as procedurally efficient --- it avoided the need to relitigate confidentiality designations from scratch in a new proceeding and ensured an orderly transition.
70	
71	**In Galveston Health / Meridian (Matter B, Docket No. 9428),** the bridge provision included an additional **\"public filing\" restriction**: any party --- or the FTC itself --- seeking to file materials designated as Confidential or Highly Confidential on a public record in the subsequent proceeding was required to provide the producing party with at least seven business days\' prior written notice and a reasonable opportunity to seek an order from the presiding tribunal restricting public access. This notice requirement provides the producing party with a meaningful opportunity to protect its most sensitive materials before they are exposed on a public docket.
72	
73	**Recommendation:** We should propose adding a bridge provision modeled on Matter C\'s Paragraph 21, with the additional public-filing notice requirement drawn from Matter B. This is a critical client-protection measure and should be treated as a **high-priority** negotiation item. Our notes from the April 8 call reflect that Staff showed some openness to discussing the \"transition\" to any subsequent proceeding, and we should capitalize on that signal. The bridge provision is also a natural complement to the three-tier confidentiality structure discussed in Section VII below, as it ensures that the highest-tier designations carry through into any enforcement action.
74	
75	**[VI. Expert and Consultant Conflicts Screening]{.underline}**
76	
77	Paragraph 8 of the proposed order permits outside experts and consultants retained by any party to access Confidential Information and Highly Confidential Information upon executing a standard acknowledgment and agreement form attached as Exhibit B to the proposed order. However, the proposed order imposes no requirement that the expert or consultant be screened for conflicts of interest prior to receiving access. Specifically, there is no requirement to confirm that the expert or consultant (a) has not provided consulting services to a competitor of the producing party in the same industry segment within the preceding twenty-four months, or (b) will not provide such services during the pendency of the investigation.
78	
79	This gap presents a concrete and meaningful risk in the context of the Whitmore/Cascade investigation. Whitmore has retained Northbridge Economics Group as its economic consultant to assist with the FTC\'s review. Cascade and the FTC may also retain economic experts with experience in the freight, logistics, and transportation sectors. The universe of qualified economic experts with relevant industry experience in regional freight and last-mile delivery is relatively small, and there is a meaningful possibility that an expert retained by the opposing party or by FTC Staff has recently consulted for, or is currently consulting for, a direct competitor of Whitmore or Cascade in one or more of the overlap markets. An expert who has access to Highly Confidential pricing data, customer-level profitability information, route-level cost structures, or the \"Project Atlas\" board materials --- and who simultaneously has, or recently had, a consulting relationship with a competitor --- creates an unacceptable risk of information leakage. Even absent intentional disclosure, an expert\'s thinking and analytical approach can be influenced by exposure to a party\'s most sensitive competitive intelligence, and that influence can manifest in subsequent engagements for competitors.
80	
81	**In Galveston Health / Meridian (Matter B, Docket No. 9428),** which involved similarly sensitive patient-pricing data and proprietary econometric models, the parties negotiated an expert conflicts screening provision requiring that: (a) before any expert or consultant is given access to Confidential or Highly Confidential Information, the retaining party must provide the producing party with the expert\'s name, firm affiliation, and a written disclosure identifying any consulting engagements for companies that compete with the producing party within the prior twenty-four months; (b) the producing party has **five business days** from receipt of the disclosure to object to the expert on conflict grounds; and (c) if the objection is not resolved by agreement within an additional five business days, either party may raise the dispute with FTC Staff for informal resolution. FTC Staff accepted this provision after minor revisions to the timeline.
82	
83	**In Thornfield / Beckett (Matter A, Docket No. 9412),** a similar but less detailed provision was negotiated, requiring only a general conflicts disclosure and a **three-business-day** objection period. The shorter timeline proved unworkable in practice --- counsel reported difficulty completing conflicts checks within three days, particularly where the expert\'s firm had multiple offices and a broad client base --- and the parties informally agreed to extend the objection period on a case-by-case basis.
84	
85	Both Matter A and Matter B included a **forward-looking restriction**: the expert or consultant was prohibited from consulting for any competitor of the producing party in the same industry segment during the pendency of the investigation and for a period of twelve months after the investigation\'s conclusion, with respect to any matter in which the expert could use or benefit from information obtained under the protective order. This forward-looking component is essential to ensuring that the conflicts screening is not merely a snapshot-in-time exercise but provides enduring protection.
86	
87	**Recommendation:** We should propose adding a conflicts-screening provision modeled on Matter B, with a five-business-day objection window, a twenty-four-month lookback period, and a forward-looking restriction covering the pendency of the investigation plus twelve months. This provision is directly relevant to the engagement of Northbridge Economics Group and to any experts that Cascade or FTC Staff may retain. We should prepare a draft provision for inclusion in our markup to FTC Staff.
88	
89	**[VII. Three-Tier Confidentiality Structure]{.underline}**
90	
91	The proposed order establishes only two tiers of confidentiality protection: \"Confidential Information\" and \"Highly Confidential Information --- Outside Counsel Only.\" In major HSR merger investigations involving direct competitors with significant market overlaps, market practice has increasingly moved toward a three-tier system that adds a \"Restricted Highly Confidential --- Attorneys\' Eyes Only\" (or equivalent) super-tier above the existing two tiers. The proposed order\'s two-tier structure is insufficient for this investigation.
92	
93	The need for a third tier arises from the nature of the competitive relationship between Whitmore and Cascade and the extraordinary sensitivity of certain categories of information that will be produced. Whitmore and Cascade are direct competitors in regional freight and last-mile delivery in the Pacific Northwest and Northern California. Certain categories of information are so competitively sensitive that even disclosure to outside economic experts --- who, despite any conflicts screening, are practitioners with deep industry relationships and ongoing engagement portfolios --- creates an unacceptable risk of competitive harm. Specifically:
94	
95	> • Whitmore\'s \"Project Atlas: Western Expansion Strategy\" (a 2023 board presentation), which discusses competitive dynamics, pricing strategies, and growth initiatives in each of the four overlap markets, contains forward-looking strategic intelligence that would be extraordinarily valuable to any competitor and that has been closely held within Whitmore\'s senior leadership and board.
96	>
97	> • Cascade\'s customer-level profitability data, which reflects customer-specific margins, retention economics, discount structures, and churn patterns, constitutes the core of Cascade\'s competitive positioning and pricing strategy in the overlap markets.
98	>
99	> • Any future pricing or bidding strategies, capacity expansion plans, fleet deployment models, or acquisition pipeline analyses produced by either party.
100	
101	The existing \"Highly Confidential --- Outside Counsel Only\" tier, as drafted, permits access by outside experts and consultants who execute the standard acknowledgment form. A third tier would restrict access to a small, named group of outside attorneys --- and would exclude even testifying or consulting experts --- thereby providing the highest level of protection for the most competitively sensitive materials while still permitting FTC Staff unrestricted access to conduct its review.
102	
103	In competitor-versus-competitor merger investigations, a three-tier system has become the prevailing approach. FTC Staff has accepted three-tier protective orders in multiple recent matters, recognizing that the additional tier serves the parties\' legitimate interest in protecting their most sensitive competitive intelligence while not impeding the Bureau\'s investigative function.
104	
105	**In Thornfield / Beckett (Matter A, Docket No. 9412),** the parties negotiated a three-tier system. The third tier was labeled \"Restricted Confidential --- Outside Counsel Only\" and limited access to no more than **four named outside attorneys** per party, plus their litigation support staff who signed individual acknowledgment forms. Testifying experts were excluded from access to third-tier materials. FTC Staff retained unrestricted access to all three tiers. The modification was accepted by Staff in Mergers II.
106	
107	**In Crestline / Durango (Matter C, Docket No. 9435),** the three-tier system used a slightly different nomenclature and structure. The third tier was designated \"Attorneys\' Eyes Only\" and required the producing party to specifically designate materials at this level on a document-by-document or category basis. Access was limited to **three named outside attorneys** per side. Importantly, the FTC agreed that materials designated at the third tier would receive the same treatment --- including the same access restrictions --- in any subsequent administrative proceeding under Part III. Staff in Mergers IV accepted this structure, making it directly applicable precedent for our matter.
108	
109	A three-tier structure requires careful definition of the categories of information eligible for the highest designation, to prevent overdesignation that could impede the parties\' ability to effectively participate in the investigation. In both Matter A and Matter C, the protective orders included **illustrative categories** of information appropriate for third-tier designation --- such as forward-looking strategic plans, customer-specific pricing models, pending bid proposals, non-public acquisition pipeline documents, and internal competitive assessments --- while preserving the designating party\'s discretion to designate additional materials at the third tier subject to the existing challenge procedures.
110	
111	**Recommendation:** We should propose adding a third tier --- \"Restricted Highly Confidential --- Attorneys\' Eyes Only\" --- modeled on the structure accepted in Matter C. Access should be limited to three named outside attorneys per party, plus FTC Staff without restriction. Testifying and consulting experts should be excluded. The proposal should include illustrative categories such as \"Project Atlas\" materials, customer-level profitability data, forward-looking strategic and pricing analyses, and non-public acquisition pipeline documents. Matter C provides direct Mergers IV precedent and should be cited prominently. This should be treated as a **high-priority** negotiation item, consistent with the instructions we received from David Pratt, General Counsel of Whitmore, at our April 4 meeting.
112	
113	**[VIII. Derivative Materials Provision]{.underline}**
114	
115	The proposed order governs access to, and the return or destruction of, Confidential Information and Highly Confidential Information but does not address how such information may be referenced, quoted, summarized, or incorporated in **derivative materials** --- including expert reports, white papers, economic analyses, declarations, submissions to the FTC, or internal memoranda prepared by counsel or their agents. This omission creates a significant gap in the protective framework.
116	
117	Consider a practical example: if Whitmore\'s economic expert, Northbridge Economics Group, prepares a white paper for submission to FTC Staff analyzing competitive conditions in the overlap markets and that white paper references or incorporates Cascade\'s Highly Confidential customer-level pricing data, there is no mechanism in the proposed order to ensure that the white paper itself is treated as Highly Confidential. The same risk exists in reverse --- if Cascade\'s experts prepare an analysis that references or synthesizes data from Whitmore\'s \"Project Atlas\" materials in a submission or presentation, the proposed order provides no basis for requiring that the derivative analysis carry the same designation as the source materials.
118	
119	Without a derivative materials provision, a party could effectively downgrade the protection level of the most sensitive information by incorporating it --- whether in summary form, through direct quotation, or through analytical synthesis --- into a lower-designated or entirely undesignated work product. This creates a backdoor around the confidentiality tiers and undermines the integrity of the protective order\'s entire tiered structure. The risk is compounded in an investigation of this scale, where economic experts will be preparing complex analyses drawing on data from multiple sources and multiple designation levels.
120	
121	**In Galveston Health / Meridian (Matter B, Docket No. 9428),** the protective order included a **\"derivative materials\" provision** (Paragraph 13 of that order) stating that: (a) any document, analysis, report, memorandum, declaration, or other material that incorporates, reflects, is derived from, or is based upon Confidential or Highly Confidential Information shall automatically receive the highest confidentiality designation level of any source material referenced or utilized in its preparation; (b) the author of the derivative material must mark it with the appropriate confidentiality designation and treat it accordingly; and (c) the derivative material is subject to the same access restrictions, handling requirements, and return or destruction obligations as the underlying source material from which it derives. FTC Staff accepted this provision without material negotiation, recognizing that it was a logical corollary of the tiered confidentiality system.
122	
123	**In Thornfield / Beckett (Matter A, Docket No. 9412),** a less detailed version of the provision was included, simply stating that \"notes, summaries, or extracts\" of confidential materials are subject to the same protections as the underlying materials. The broader language used in Matter B is preferable because it captures the full range of derivative works --- including econometric analyses, regression models, and expert reports that synthesize data from multiple sources in ways that may not be immediately recognizable as derived from any single document.
124	
125	In the context of this investigation, a robust derivative materials provision is essential. Northbridge Economics Group will be preparing economic analyses using Whitmore\'s own data and, potentially, data produced by Cascade in the course of the investigation. If the FTC shares such analyses internally or uses them in any subsequent enforcement proceeding, the absence of a derivative materials provision could result in the exposure of competitively sensitive information that the producing party designated at the highest tier. This provision also interacts directly with the proposed three-tier confidentiality structure discussed in Section VII above: if source materials are designated at the third tier --- \"Restricted Highly Confidential --- Attorneys\' Eyes Only\" --- then any derivative materials based on those sources must receive the same designation and be subject to the same access restrictions.
126	
127	**Recommendation:** We should propose adding a derivative materials provision modeled on Matter B\'s Paragraph 13, with the additional clarification that derivative materials based on third-tier source materials automatically receive third-tier designation. This is a **medium-priority** item but one that is essential to supporting the integrity of the overall tiered confidentiality structure. Without it, the three-tier system proposed in Section VII would be incomplete.
128	
129	**[IX. Summary of Recommendations and Priority Assessment]{.underline}**
130	
131	The following table summarizes the six areas of recommended modification, the specific paragraphs of the proposed protective order affected, the precedent support for each modification, the estimated likelihood of FTC Staff acceptance, and the priority level assigned to each item.
132	
133	  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
134	  **\#**      **Issue**                                     **Paragraph(s) Affected**              **Precedent Support**   **Estimated Staff Flexibility**                              **Priority**
135	  ----------- --------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------- ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ -----------------
136	  1           Three-tier confidentiality structure          Paras. 3, 7, 8                         Matters A, C            Medium --- accepted in Mergers IV in Matter C                **High**
137	
138	  2           FRE 502(d) clawback protections               Para. 16                               Matters A, C            Medium-High --- accepted in Mergers IV in Matter C           **High**
139	
140	  3           Bridge provision for subsequent proceedings   New paragraph (proposed as Para. 23)   Matters B, C            Medium --- Staff showed some openness on April 8 call        **High**
141	
142	  4           Challenge procedure deadline extension        Para. 18                               Matters A, B            High --- Staff signaled flexibility on April 8 call          **Medium-High**
143	
144	  5           Expert and consultant conflicts screening     Para. 8                                Matters A, B            Medium --- accepted after negotiation in both precedents     **Medium**
145	
146	  6           Derivative materials provision                New paragraph (proposed as Para. 24)   Matters A, B            High --- accepted without material negotiation in Matter B   **Medium**
147	  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
148	
149	These six issues are part of a broader set of proposed modifications that Kate Ashford\'s team is developing for submission to FTC Staff. Additional modifications --- relating to in-house counsel screening procedures, inter-agency sharing provisions under 15 U.S.C. § 46(f), the definition of \"conclusion of the investigation\" for purposes of the return/destruction obligations, FTC Staff separation and rotation concerns, the treatment of third-party materials produced by Ridgeline Capital Partners (Cascade\'s majority shareholder), and the definition of \"Highly Confidential Information\" to expressly encompass structured data sets --- are addressed in separate analyses but are reinforced by the precedents discussed in this memorandum.
150	
151	We recommend coordinating with Pemberton & Locke LLP (Alan Hsiao, lead partner for Cascade) and Grayson Mills LLP (Robert Tanaka, counsel for Ridgeline Capital Partners) to present a **unified markup** to FTC Staff well in advance of the April 25, 2025 deadline. A unified submission will carry significantly more weight than uncoordinated individual proposals and will signal to Staff that the requested modifications reflect a considered, consensus position rather than aggressive over-reaching by any single party.
152	
153	The strongest negotiating posture is to present all modifications as a **comprehensive package**, citing the precedents from Mergers IV --- particularly Matter C (*Crestline / Durango*, Docket No. 9435) --- as especially persuasive given that the same division is handling the Whitmore/Cascade investigation. Where modifications have already been accepted by Staff in Mergers IV, there is a strong basis for arguing that consistency and predictability counsel in favor of adopting the same approach here.
154	
155	**[X. Conclusion]{.underline}**
156	
157	The three precedent matters analyzed in this memorandum demonstrate that FTC Staff --- including Staff in the Mergers IV Division handling our matter --- has accepted modifications beyond the standard-form protective order in each of the six areas addressed above. The modifications we recommend are not novel or untested proposals; they are consistent with the evolving market practice in HSR merger investigations involving direct competitors with substantial market overlaps and large-scale document productions.
158	
159	I am prepared to draft proposed language for each of the six modifications for your review and to coordinate with co-counsel at Pemberton & Locke and Grayson Mills to develop a unified markup for submission to FTC Staff. I am also available to discuss any of these issues further at your convenience. All underlying protective orders from the three precedent matters, including the fully executed final versions and the redline negotiation histories, are available in the HSW antitrust precedent database (file references: TPO-9412-A, TPO-9428-B, TPO-9435-C) for reference.
160	
161	*This memorandum is intended solely for internal use by Hargrove, Stern & Whitfield LLP attorneys and staff working on FTC File No. 241-0187. Distribution to any person outside the firm, including co-counsel and the client, requires prior authorization from the responsible partner.*
162

**PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

**Call Notes --- Joint Conference Call with FTC Staff re Proposed Protective Order**

**Matter:** Whitmore Logistics Holdings, Inc. / Cascade Regional Freight, Inc. --- FTC File No. 241-0187

**Date/Time:** Tuesday, April 8, 2025, 2:00 PM -- 3:15 PM (Eastern)

**Prepared by:** Benjamin Torres, Senior Associate, Hargrove, Stern & Whitfield LLP

**Format:** Conference bridge (dial-in); no videoconference

**[1. Participants]{.underline}**

**FTC Bureau of Competition, Mergers IV Division:**

> • Jonathan Heller, Lead Staff Attorney
>
> • Rebecca Muñoz, Assistant Director
>
> • Two additional Staff attorneys (names not captured; one identified herself as an economist)

**Hargrove, Stern & Whitfield LLP (counsel for Whitmore Logistics Holdings, Inc.):**

> • Catherine (\"Kate\") Ashford, Partner
>
> • Benjamin Torres, Senior Associate

**Pemberton & Locke LLP (counsel for Cascade Regional Freight, Inc.):**

> • Alan Hsiao, Partner

**Not on the call:** Robert Tanaka, Grayson Mills LLP (counsel for Ridgeline Capital Partners, LLC, Whitmore\'s majority equity sponsor). At the outset of the call, Ashford noted that Whitmore had received informal concerns from Ridgeline\'s counsel and might raise certain third-party-related issues during the discussion.

**[2. Opening / General Framework]{.underline}**

Ashford opened by thanking Staff for circulating the proposed protective order on April 2, 2025, and noted that both Whitmore and Cascade had completed initial reviews. She emphasized that the parties appreciate Staff\'s willingness to discuss potential modifications on the call and stated that the shared goal is to reach a joint agreed order by the April 25, 2025 submission deadline.

Heller responded that the FTC\'s proposed form order reflects the Commission\'s \"strong institutional preference\" for its standard template but acknowledged that \"reasonable modifications consistent with the Commission\'s interests\" would be considered. Muñoz added that in her experience, the standard form has been used in the \"vast majority\" of recent merger investigations but confirmed Staff\'s willingness to hear specific concerns from both sides.

Hsiao, on behalf of Cascade, echoed Ashford\'s comments and stated that Cascade has \"particular sensitivity around customer-level profitability data and pricing models\" that it wants to ensure receive the highest level of protection under the order.

*Torres note: Tone was cordial but Staff was clearly signaling they will resist wholesale departures from the template. We should pick our battles carefully.*

**[3. Discussion of Paragraph 14 --- Sharing with DOJ and State Attorneys General]{.underline}**

Ashford raised concerns about Paragraph 14, which permits the FTC to share Confidential Information with the DOJ Antitrust Division and state attorneys general \"as the Commission deems appropriate\" without prior notice to the producing party. Ashford stated that Whitmore\'s position is that the producing party should receive advance written notice --- she proposed ten business days --- before any such disclosure, and that the receiving agency should be required to agree in writing to be bound by the protective order\'s terms before receiving any materials. She further noted that without a notice mechanism, the producing party has no opportunity to seek judicial protection if it believes specific materials should not be shared, a concern that is particularly acute in an investigation involving direct competitors exchanging sensitive competitive information.

Heller\'s response was firm. He stated that Paragraph 14 \"reflects longstanding Commission practice and interagency cooperation agreements\" and that \"this provision is non-negotiable.\" He said the FTC cannot agree to any prior-notice requirement that would, in his words, \"create a de facto veto over the Commission\'s ability to coordinate with sister enforcement agencies.\"

Muñoz reinforced this, stating she has \"never agreed to a prior-notice requirement in Paragraph 14 in any matter\" during her tenure.

Hsiao supported Ashford\'s position, noting Cascade\'s concern that state AG offices may not have adequate confidentiality protections and that pricing data shared with a state AG in, say, Oregon or Washington could end up accessible to state-level officials with connections to regional competitors in the Pacific Northwest freight market.

Ashford proposed a compromise. If a prior-notice requirement is unacceptable, would Staff consider: (a) a provision requiring the FTC to use \"reasonable best efforts\" to notify the producing party before sharing; (b) a requirement that the receiving agency execute a written acknowledgment agreeing to be bound by the protective order\'s terms before receiving any materials; or (c) at minimum, a notification to the producing party within five business days after the sharing occurs?

Heller said he would \"take it back to front office\" but was \"not optimistic\" about any form of notice obligation. He did note, however, that \"as a practical matter, we typically request that receiving agencies agree to treat materials consistently with the protective order,\" suggesting some informal practice that could potentially be formalized.

*Torres note: Heller\'s language was categorical but Muñoz\'s follow-up was slightly softer (\"in any matter I have handled\"). There may be room for the written-acknowledgment-from-receiving-agency piece even if prior notice is rejected. The after-the-fact notice is probably our fallback. We should draft alternative language reflecting a spectrum of options.*

**[4. Discussion of Paragraph 19 --- Return/Destruction and \"Conclusion of the Investigation\"]{.underline}**

Ashford raised concerns about Paragraph 19, which requires return or destruction of all Confidential Information \"within 60 days of the conclusion of the investigation\" but does not define \"conclusion of the investigation.\" She noted the ambiguity: the investigation could conclude in multiple ways --- (1) Staff recommends closing the investigation and the Commission closes the file; (2) the parties enter into a consent decree; (3) the FTC files an administrative complaint (Part III proceeding); (4) the FTC seeks a preliminary injunction in federal court under Section 13(b); or (5) the transaction is abandoned by the parties. Each scenario has different implications for when the 60-day clock starts.

Ashford specifically flagged the scenario where the FTC issues an administrative complaint: \"If the Commission issues a complaint and the matter proceeds to administrative litigation, the materials will still be relevant and needed. A return/destruction obligation triggered by the \'conclusion\' of the pre-complaint investigation would be unworkable if litigation follows.\"

Heller acknowledged this is a \"fair point\" and stated Staff would be \"open to adding some definitional clarity.\" He suggested that \"conclusion\" could be defined as the earliest of (a) written notification by Staff that the investigation has been closed, (b) entry of a consent order, or (c) expiration or abandonment of the transaction --- but was less clear about what happens if administrative or judicial proceedings follow.

Muñoz stated she has seen orders in other matters that include a \"carve-out\" where, if the matter transitions to administrative litigation or a federal court action, the protective order\'s terms remain in effect --- including material retention rights --- until a successor protective order is entered in the litigation.

Hsiao agreed with Ashford\'s concerns and suggested that the definition should also clarify that withdrawal of the HSR filing or expiration of the Merger Agreement outside date (October 31, 2025, or the extended date of January 29, 2026) would trigger the 60-day clock.

*Torres note: Staff signaled clear flexibility here. Heller\'s proposed three-part definition is a good starting point but incomplete --- we need to address the administrative litigation scenario. Muñoz\'s \"carve-out\" comment is very helpful; we should draft a bridge provision. This should be an easy win if we draft reasonable language.*

**[5. Discussion of FTC Staff Definition and Economist Rotation]{.underline}**

Ashford raised concerns about the definition of \"FTC Staff\" in Paragraph 2(f), which includes \"all employees and contractors of the Federal Trade Commission assigned to FTC File No. 241-0187,\" and noted the absence of any restriction on the subsequent use or retention of confidential information by FTC Staff --- particularly economists --- who leave the agency during or after the investigation.

Ashford stated that Whitmore\'s client has \"specific and heightened concerns\" about the risk that an FTC economist who reviews the parties\' most sensitive pricing data and strategic documents --- including Whitmore\'s \"Project Atlas: Western Expansion Strategy\" board presentation --- could depart the Commission and join a private economic consulting firm that consults for Whitmore\'s or Cascade\'s competitors in the freight and last-mile delivery industry.

Ashford proposed two potential solutions: (a) require FTC Staff members who access Highly Confidential Information to execute individual acknowledgment forms, with a provision that post-separation use or disclosure of such information is prohibited; or (b) at minimum, require the FTC to notify the producing party if a Staff member who accessed Highly Confidential Information leaves the agency within 12 months of such access.

Heller\'s response was measured but cautious. He stated that \"the Commission takes its obligations to protect confidential information seriously\" and that \"departing employees are subject to government ethics obligations,\" but he was \"not in a position to agree to individual acknowledgment forms for FTC Staff\" because the Commission does not typically submit its own employees to party-drafted acknowledgment requirements. He stated this would need to be \"elevated internally.\"

Muñoz noted that there are existing federal ethics rules and statutes --- including 18 U.S.C. § 1905 and applicable OGE regulations --- that restrict departing government employees\' use of nonpublic information, and suggested that \"duplication\" in the protective order might be \"unnecessary.\"

Hsiao stated Cascade shares these concerns, particularly because Cascade\'s customer-level profitability data \"is the crown jewel of our business\" and Cascade has only a small number of direct competitors in its 11-state Western operating territory.

*Torres note: Staff\'s response was not a flat no --- Heller said it needs to be \"elevated,\" which suggests front-office involvement. Muñoz\'s cite to existing ethics obligations is a soft deflection; those rules protect government interests, not necessarily the producing parties\' private commercial interests. We may not get individual acknowledgment forms, but a notification-upon-departure provision is worth pushing hard for. Should flag for Kate that this is a medium-difficulty ask --- harder than Paragraph 19, easier than Paragraph 14.*

**[6. Other Issues Discussed (Brief Summary)]{.underline}**

**Challenge procedure deadline (Paragraph 18).** Ashford raised the 10-business-day deadline for filing a motion challenging a confidentiality designation. She noted the anticipated combined production volume of approximately 1.88 million documents across 76 custodians and argued that 10 business days is insufficient for meaningful review and challenge. Heller said Staff \"would consider a modest extension\" and asked what the parties would propose. Ashford suggested 20 business days. Heller said he \"could probably work with 15 or 20 business days\" as long as designations remain in effect during the pendency of any challenge. *Torres note: Essentially agreed --- draft at 20 business days with a \"designations remain in effect\" provision.*

**In-house counsel access (Paragraph 7(b)).** Hsiao flagged the lack of a screening procedure for in-house counsel who access Highly Confidential materials. Heller stated the three-person cap is standard and Staff\'s preference is not to \"over-proceduralize\" access, but he acknowledged that \"if the parties want to add a notice-and-objection mechanism, that\'s between the parties\" and Staff would not object if both sides agree. *Torres note: Staff neutral --- this is a party-to-party negotiation. Need to coordinate with Pemberton & Locke.*

**Expert/consultant conflicts (Paragraph 8).** Ashford briefly mentioned the absence of any conflicts-check requirement for outside experts and consultants who receive access to Confidential or Highly Confidential materials. Heller said he had \"no strong view\" on this as long as it doesn\'t \"impede Staff\'s ability to engage its own experts.\" *Torres note: Staff largely indifferent; should be easy to add.*

**Structured data and Highly Confidential tier definitions.** Ashford noted that the Highly Confidential tier definition (Paragraph 3(b)) references \"documents\" but may not clearly encompass structured data, databases, or financial models. Heller stated the definition is \"intended to be read broadly\" but said he would \"not oppose clarifying language\" if the parties want to add specific references to structured data formats. *Torres note: Easy win --- draft expanded definition.*

**[7. Scheduling and Next Steps]{.underline}**

Heller confirmed the April 25, 2025 deadline for the parties to submit either a joint proposed protective order or competing proposals. He stated a \"strong preference\" for a joint submission.

Ashford stated that HSW would circulate a redlined markup of the proposed order to Pemberton & Locke and FTC Staff \"within the next 10 days\" --- i.e., by approximately April 18, 2025. Hsiao stated that Pemberton & Locke may have additional comments beyond those discussed on the call and would coordinate with HSW before circulation to Staff.

Ashford mentioned that Ridgeline Capital Partners\' counsel (Grayson Mills LLP, Robert Tanaka) had communicated concerns about the treatment of PE sponsor materials and that the parties\' markup might include provisions addressing third-party-source designation rights. Heller stated he had \"no objection in principle\" to addressing third-party concerns but noted the protective order governs materials produced to the FTC, not the relationship between the parties and their investors.

Heller offered to schedule a follow-up call during the week of April 21 to discuss any remaining disputes before the April 25 deadline. Muñoz stated that if the parties cannot reach full agreement on all provisions, Staff would expect each side to submit its own proposed order with a brief cover letter identifying areas of disagreement and the basis for each position.

*Torres note: Timeline is tight but workable. We need to circulate our draft to Kate by April 14 at the latest to allow time for internal review, client review (David Pratt), coordination with Pemberton & Locke, and potential follow-up with Staff. Should also loop in Grayson Mills (Robert Tanaka) on the third-party provisions before we finalize.*

**[8. Action Items]{.underline}**

> • **Torres** to prepare first draft of redlined markup of FTC proposed protective order, incorporating all issues discussed on the call, for Kate Ashford\'s review by **April 14, 2025**.
>
> • **Torres** to review HSW internal memo on protective order precedents (being prepared concurrently) for supporting authority on each proposed modification.
>
> • **Ashford** to circulate draft markup to **Alan Hsiao** (Pemberton & Locke) for Cascade\'s input.
>
> • **Ashford** to share relevant portions of draft with **David Pratt** (Whitmore General Counsel) for client sign-off, particularly on in-house counsel access provisions and the FTC economist rotation issue.
>
> • **Torres** to coordinate with **Robert Tanaka** (Grayson Mills LLP) on Ridgeline-specific provisions before finalizing.
>
> • **Ashford** to propose a follow-up call date during week of April 21 to Heller.
>

**GRAYSON MILLS LLP** *Attorneys at Law*

1600 Wazee Street, Suite 2200 Denver, Colorado 80202

Telephone: (303) 555-4100 Facsimile: (303) 555-4101 www.graysonmillslaw.com

**Robert Tanaka** Partner Direct: (303) 555-4118 rtanaka@graysonmillslaw.com

April 10, 2025

Catherine \"Kate\" Ashford, Esq. Partner Hargrove, Stern & Whitfield LLP 1700 K Street NW, Suite 1200 Washington, DC 20006

Alan Hsiao, Esq. Partner Pemberton & Locke LLP 560 California Street, Suite 3400 San Francisco, CA 94104

**Re: FTC File No. 241-0187 --- Proposed Protective Order Governing Confidential Information --- Concerns of Ridgeline Capital Partners**

Dear Ms. Ashford and Mr. Hsiao:

**[I. Purpose of This Letter]{.underline}**

I write on behalf of our client, Ridgeline Capital Partners (\"Ridgeline\"), a Delaware limited partnership. Ridgeline holds an approximately 38% minority equity interest in Cascade Regional Freight, Inc. (\"Cascade\"), with the balance of Cascade\'s equity (approximately 62%) held by the Nakamura family and its related entities.

As you know, the Federal Trade Commission is conducting an investigation into the proposed acquisition of Cascade by Whitmore Logistics Holdings, Inc. (\"Whitmore\"), proceeding under FTC File No. 241-0187. On March 18, 2025, the FTC issued a Second Request to both Whitmore and Cascade in connection with that investigation. We understand that FTC Staff --- specifically Jonathan Heller, Lead Staff Attorney, Bureau of Competition, Mergers IV Division --- circulated a proposed protective order on April 2, 2025, and that counsel for the parties held a joint call with Mr. Heller on April 8, 2025, to discuss potential modifications to the proposed order. We further understand that the deadline for submission of a joint proposed protective order (or, in the alternative, competing proposals) is April 25, 2025.

The purpose of this letter is to identify Ridgeline\'s specific concerns regarding the treatment of its proprietary materials under the proposed protective order and to request that certain protections be incorporated into any order submitted to the FTC. We appreciate the opportunity to provide this input and acknowledge that Ridgeline is not a party to the investigation. Ridgeline does, however, have a direct and substantial interest in ensuring that its proprietary information --- which may be swept into Cascade\'s document production --- receives appropriate confidentiality protections.

By way of additional background, Ridgeline\'s Managing Director, Lisa Fontaine, has already discussed these concerns by telephone with Whitmore\'s General Counsel, David Pratt, and Cascade\'s General Counsel, Karen Solberg. This letter formalizes those concerns and presents them in a form suitable for consideration by counsel and, if appropriate, by FTC Staff.

**[II. Background --- Ridgeline\'s Materials at Risk]{.underline}**

In connection with the Second Request, Cascade is obligated to produce documents and information that may include materials originated by, or belonging to, Ridgeline as a significant equity holder. Many of these materials reside in Cascade\'s files solely because Ridgeline, in its capacity as a major investor and board participant, furnished them to Cascade\'s management or board of directors. Ridgeline anticipates that the following categories of proprietary materials may be responsive to the Second Request and swept into Cascade\'s production:

> 1\. **Fund Performance Data.** Ridgeline\'s fund-level financial performance information, including internal rate of return (\"IRR\") calculations, fund-level net asset values, and periodic performance reports relating to the fund or funds through which Ridgeline holds its Cascade investment. These materials reflect the aggregate performance of Ridgeline\'s investment portfolio, not merely the performance of the Cascade investment in isolation.
>
> 2\. **Limited Partner Communications.** Correspondence, reports, and presentations prepared by Ridgeline for its limited partners (\"LPs\") that reference the Cascade investment, including quarterly and annual LP updates, capital call notices, and distribution notices. These communications contain fund-level and portfolio-level financial data, LP-specific information, and forward-looking projections that are distributed under strict confidentiality obligations between Ridgeline and its investor base.
>
> 3\. **Internal Investment Committee Memoranda.** Ridgeline\'s internal investment committee memoranda and related materials prepared in connection with the original acquisition of its Cascade stake and any subsequent follow-on investment decisions. These memoranda contain proprietary deal underwriting, valuation analyses, market assessments, and strategic recommendations that reflect Ridgeline\'s investment process and analytical methodology.
>
> 4\. **IRR Calculations and Valuation Models.** Detailed financial models, including discounted cash flow analyses, comparable company analyses, and IRR/multiple-of-invested-capital projections, that reflect Ridgeline\'s proprietary valuation methodologies and assumptions. These models embody the analytical frameworks that Ridgeline applies across its portfolio and are among the most competitively sensitive materials in Ridgeline\'s possession.
>
> 5\. **Board-Level Communications.** Materials prepared by Ridgeline for Cascade\'s board of directors (on which Ridgeline has representation) that reflect Ridgeline\'s proprietary views on Cascade\'s strategy, competitive positioning, and the proposed transaction with Whitmore. These materials may contain Ridgeline\'s independent assessment of valuation, deal terms, and strategic alternatives.

We wish to emphasize that these materials are not merely sensitive business information of Cascade --- they are proprietary to Ridgeline and, in many cases, contain information about Ridgeline\'s fund operations, LP relationships, and investment strategies that have no relevance to the competitive analysis the FTC is conducting. Disclosure of fund performance data, LP communications, and IRR calculations could cause significant competitive harm to Ridgeline in the private equity market, as this information could reveal fund performance, investment strategy, and LP relationships to competing private equity firms, potential co-investors, and other market participants.

**[III. Deficiencies in the Proposed Protective Order]{.underline}**

I have reviewed the FTC\'s proposed protective order circulated on April 2, 2025, in its entirety (22 numbered paragraphs, 18 pages). While we recognize that the proposed order reflects the FTC\'s standard form and is designed to balance investigative needs with legitimate confidentiality interests, Ridgeline has identified the following specific deficiencies from its perspective as an originating third party:

> 1\. **No Third-Party Designation Rights.** The proposed order contemplates only the \"Producing Party\" --- defined implicitly as the party responding to the Second Request (*i.e.*, Whitmore or Cascade) --- as having the right to designate materials as \"Confidential\" or \"Highly Confidential --- Outside Counsel Only.\" Ridgeline, as the originator of many of the materials Cascade will produce, has no independent right under the proposed order to designate its own materials at the appropriate confidentiality tier. This is a significant structural gap.
>
> 2\. **No Notice Before Redesignation or Disclosure.** The proposed order\'s challenge procedure (Paragraph 18) permits a receiving party to challenge a confidentiality designation, but there is no provision requiring that Ridgeline --- as the originating third party --- receive notice before any party or the FTC seeks to redesignate or disclose Ridgeline\'s proprietary materials. Under the current framework, Ridgeline\'s materials could be downgraded from \"Highly Confidential --- Outside Counsel Only\" to \"Confidential\" without Ridgeline\'s knowledge or consent.
>
> 3\. **Dependency on Cascade\'s Designations.** Under the proposed order, Ridgeline would be entirely dependent on Cascade to designate Ridgeline\'s materials at the appropriate confidentiality level. While Ridgeline maintains a cooperative relationship with Cascade and its counsel at Pemberton & Locke LLP, Ridgeline\'s interests are not identical to Cascade\'s. Cascade may not fully appreciate the sensitivity of fund-level financial data from Ridgeline\'s perspective, and Cascade\'s designation decisions will naturally be guided by Cascade\'s own litigation and regulatory posture.
>
> 4\. **Two-Tier System May Be Insufficient.** The proposed order\'s two tiers --- \"Confidential\" and \"Highly Confidential --- Outside Counsel Only\" --- may be insufficient to protect Ridgeline\'s most sensitive materials. Ridgeline\'s IRR calculations, fund performance data, and LP communications are among the most closely guarded categories of information in the private equity industry and warrant the highest possible level of protection.

We also note that the proposed order permits sharing of materials with the Department of Justice Antitrust Division and state attorneys general (Paragraph 14), as well as disclosure to in-house counsel of the parties (Paragraph 7(b)) and retained experts and consultants (Paragraph 8). None of these provisions includes any mechanism by which Ridgeline, as an originating third party, would be heard or afforded an opportunity to object before its materials are disseminated to additional recipients.

**[IV. Requested Protections]{.underline}**

Ridgeline respectfully requests that the following provisions be incorporated into any protective order submitted to the FTC on or before the April 25, 2025 deadline:

> 1\. **Independent Designation Rights for Third-Party Sources.** A provision expressly allowing any third party whose materials are produced in connection with the investigation --- including but not limited to Ridgeline --- to independently designate the confidentiality level of its own materials. Where the third party\'s designation differs from the Producing Party\'s designation, the higher designation should control pending resolution of any dispute.
>
> 2\. **Notice Before Redesignation or Disclosure.** A provision requiring that any party seeking to challenge the confidentiality designation of third-party-originated materials must provide at least ten (10) business days\' prior written notice to the originating third party (or its counsel of record) before initiating the challenge procedure under the protective order. The originating third party should have standing to participate in any challenge proceeding and to be heard before any tribunal adjudicating the dispute.
>
> 3\. **Notice Before Disclosure to Government Agencies.** To the extent the protective order permits the FTC to share materials with the DOJ Antitrust Division or state attorneys general, Ridgeline requests that originating third parties receive the same prior written notice as the Producing Party before any such disclosure of their materials. This notice should be provided sufficiently in advance to allow the third party a meaningful opportunity to seek additional protections if warranted.
>
> 4\. **Acknowledgment Form for Third-Party Materials.** A requirement that any person who accesses third-party-originated materials --- including in-house counsel, experts, consultants, and government personnel --- sign an acknowledgment form that specifically identifies the materials as third-party-originated and imposes the same restrictions and obligations applicable to the highest tier of confidentiality under the order.
>
> 5\. **Return/Destruction Obligation for Third-Party Materials.** The return or destruction obligations under the protective order should extend to all copies of Ridgeline\'s materials held by any party or recipient, and Ridgeline should receive direct written confirmation of return or destruction --- not solely through Cascade or its counsel.

We wish to emphasize that these requested provisions are narrowly tailored and do not impede the FTC\'s investigative functions in any respect. They are designed solely to ensure that Ridgeline --- the originator of the materials at issue --- has appropriate visibility into and control over the confidentiality protections afforded to its proprietary information. We understand that provisions substantially similar to those requested here have been accepted in other FTC merger investigations involving third-party investor materials, and we believe they reflect sound practice in matters of this nature.

Ridgeline is fully prepared to work cooperatively with Hargrove, Stern & Whitfield, Pemberton & Locke, and FTC Staff to finalize appropriate language for each of the requested provisions.

**[V. Closing]{.underline}**

Given that the deadline for submission of a joint proposed protective order is April 25, 2025, we respectfully request that you give this letter prompt attention. Ridgeline is willing to participate in any further discussions or calls with FTC Staff, and Grayson Mills LLP is prepared to appear on behalf of Ridgeline in any protective order negotiations if that would be helpful to the process.

We would appreciate it if each of you could confirm receipt of this letter and indicate whether you are amenable to incorporating Ridgeline\'s requested provisions into the joint proposed protective order. Should you find it useful, we are prepared to provide proposed draft language for each of the five provisions described above upon request.

Ridgeline reserves all rights to seek additional protections if circumstances warrant, including the right to petition the FTC directly for relief if the parties are unable to reach agreement on appropriate provisions for third-party materials.

Thank you for your attention to these matters and for your cooperation. We look forward to working with you to resolve these concerns in advance of the April 25 deadline.

Very truly yours,

GRAYSON MILLS LLP

By: **\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_**

Robert Tanaka Partner

cc: Lisa Fontaine, Managing Director, Ridgeline Capital Partners

> Karen Solberg, General Counsel, Cascade Regional Freight, Inc. David Pratt, General Counsel, Whitmore Logistics Holdings, Inc.
